Tech Report: 10 Fighting Games That Totally Reinvent Themselves Halfway Through

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I am a full-time fighting game enthusiast.
  • According to recent reports, having played countless fighting games over the years, a handful stand out for how dramatically they shift their rules, mechanics, or entire structure mid-match, mid-mode, or halfway through a campaign.
  • According to recent reports, I grew up alongside Goku and his friends, sinking hundreds of hours into every Dragon Ball game on the PlayStation 2 and PS4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am a full-time fighting game enthusiast. I thrive on those intense, white-knuckle matches that push my skills to the limit—even when I have to retry a tough fight over and over. Honestly, half the magic lies in that process of adapting until you finally break through the wall. Beyond pure mechanics, though, I have a special soft spot for titles that refuse to stay boxed in, introducing new rules and systems as you progress until they practically reinvent themselves halfway through.

According to recent reports, having played countless fighting games over the years, a handful stand out for how dramatically they shift their rules, mechanics, or entire structure mid-match, mid-mode, or halfway through a campaign. They genuinely caught me off guard when I first played them, keeping the experience fresh instead of letting it settle into a predictable loop. Here are 10 fighting games that pull off that kind of reinvention, ranked from the cleverest twists to the most radical genre-bending shifts.

According to recent reports, I grew up alongside Goku and his friends, sinking hundreds of hours into every Dragon Ball game on the PlayStation 2 and PS4. Naturally, I nearly teared up with excitement when Dragon Ball: Sparking! ZERO was confirmed—and once I finally got my hands on it, the combat immediately won me over, recapturing the spirit of Dragon Ball Z: Budokai Tenkaichi 3 with sharper visuals and an expanded roster.

Recent findings suggest that as I dove deeper into its Episode Battle campaign, however, I realized it wasn't just retreading familiar manga and anime arcs. By fulfilling specific hidden objectives mid-fight—like defeating an opponent within a strict time limit or making an unexpected choice—you unlock Sparking! Episodes, which act as full-fledged "What If?" timelines that rewrite the rest of that character's campaign. Seeing the story branch off into uncharted territory made clearing the main mode feel far more exciting than simply replaying the same plot beats we all know by heart.

Industry observers note that I have been a die-hard fan of Jin Kazama's saga ever since I first booted up Tekken 3 on the original PlayStation, and I've played nearly every entry since—including Tekken 7 on PS4 (following its 2015 arcade debut). Beyond bringing an expanded roster and memorable newcomers to the table, it also shook up the formula halfway through its main story campaign to give the climax far more dramatic weight.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the first half of The Mishima Saga, the game sticks to the series' classic blueprint: straightforward one-on-one bouts fought under standard Tekken rules. Once Heihachi reclaims the Mishima Zaibatsu in the second half, though, the campaign throws traditional tournament rules out the window in favor of boss encounters featuring super armor phases, special EX and Rage meters, health regeneration, and mid-fight Quick-Time Events that turn battles into cinematic spectacles. Those mechanics completely changed how I approached the late-game fights, forcing me to play much more defensively so I wouldn't enter the next phase with a depleted health bar.

Mortal Kombat is another legendary franchise that has delivered decades of over-the-top violence, though narrative fatigue and identity challenges eventually pushed NetherRealm Studios to hit the reset button with Mortal Kombat 1.

Industry observers note that I placed Mortal Kombat 1 here because of how dramatically it flips both its narrative tone and its opponent design in the final stretch of its Story Mode. Across the first 14 chapters, the campaign presents a relatively grounded reboot centered on martial arts tournaments and political intrigue within Liu Kang's Latest Era.

Once the story reaches its climax at the Pyramid of Argus, however, the multiverse blows wide open and pits you against procedurally generated hybrid fighters that mash up the appearances, special moves, and Fatalities of two different characters into one. Facing off against unpredictable fusions completely changes how you read opponents on the fly, turning the finale into a chaotic, anything-goes brawl.

Sources indicate that another absolute favorite from my old PS2 days—and one I would love to see get a proper remake or sequel—is Def Jam: Fight for NY. It let you build your own custom brawler and drop straight into a gritty turf war packed with betrayals, brutal environmental knockouts, and some of the biggest hip-hop icons of the era.

According to recent reports, what really hooked me in its Story Mode was how your moveset evolves halfway through the climb. You start by creating your fighter and picking a single base discipline from five options: Martial Arts, Wrestling, Submissions, Kickboxing, or Streetfighting. Later on, by training at Stapleton Athletics gym, you unlock the ability to buy and fuse up to three distinct fighting styles onto your character—completely rewriting your combo strings, counters, and Blazin' finishers depending on the exact styles you combine.

You can't talk about standout modern fighting games without bringing up Street Fighter 6, a title I have easily poured dozens of hours into. Much like the other entries on this list, its single-player journey gradually reinvents itself into something far wilder than its opening hours suggest.

According to recent reports, early on in World Tour, you control a rookie avatar roaming Metro City with a bare-bones moveset while learning the fundamentals of the Drive System. Once you travel to Nayshall and start training under multiple Masters from the main roster, however, the mode opens up into a full-blown hybrid moveset sandbox. Before long, you can mix and match special moves from completely incompatible archetypes—pairing Ryu's Hadoken with Zangief's Spinning Piledriver and Chun-Li's kicks—exclusively within World Tour and the Battle Hub.

Unlike most games on this list, Nidhogg reinvents its genre dynamically in the middle of every single match. Each bout begins in the center of the stage as a tense, minimalist one-on-one fencing duel where spacing, blade height, and timely disarms mean everything.

According to recent reports, the moment one player scores a kill, though, the game instantly mutates from a methodical duel into a frantic obstacle-course platformer. The winner has to sprint across multiple screens toward their goal while the defeated player repeatedly respawns ahead to stop them using any dirty trick available—from dive kicks to throwing their sword—flipping attacker and defender roles back and forth until someone finally reaches the end to be devoured by the giant Nidhogg worm.

As we climb closer to the top spot, the mid-game transformations become much more drastic. At its core, For Honor is built around its Art of Battle directional guard system, demanding careful reads in close-quarters melee duels—and in its large-scale Breach mode, the first two phases revolve around escorting or halting a battering ram.

Introduced with the Marching Fire expansion in October 2018, Breach completely changes its structure once the ram breaks through both gates. At that point, the ram disappears and the match transforms into an asymmetrical raid with limited respawn tickets, forcing the attacking team to coordinate and take down an AI-controlled Commander with massive health and area-of-effect attacks while defenders fight to keep him alive—turning tactical skirmishes into a high-stakes team raid.

Originally released in arcades in 1996 before finally reaching modern consoles and PC in 2022 via Capcom Fighting Collection, although it's one of those games from the Japanese company that desperately needs a remake. Red Earth (known as Warzard in Japan) took a wildly unconventional approach to the genre. Rather than pitting you against a traditional lineup of rival fighters, it built its main Quest Mode around full-fledged RPG progression.

It kicks off like a classic Capcom 2D fighter with a striking dark-fantasy aesthetic, letting you choose from four heroes, before quickly shifting into a boss-rush RPG. As you clear battles, your character earns experience, levels up, unlocks latest special moves, and picks up elemental orbs and weapons off the ground to survive multi-phase encounters against towering monsters that mutate and change their attack patterns mid-fight.

According to recent reports, super Smash Bros. Brawl remains a beloved favorite for many fans, and its main campaign pulled off a full-blown genre switch in its second act. Throughout the first half of The Subspace Emissary, the mode plays like a linear, side-scrolling beat 'em up broken into distinct stages with rotating pairs of heroes—a straightforward formula I genuinely enjoyed.

However, once the roster finally unites in Subspace and suffers a crushing defeat at the hands of Tabuu, the entire mode transforms into The Great Maze. Suddenly, those linear stages give way to a massive, interconnected, non-linear Metroidvania-style map where you command the entire unlocked roster, rescue captured trophies, and backtrack through merged zones to rematch bosses—a sudden shift in structure that completely caught me off guard back in the day.

According to recent reports, when it comes to fighting games that radically reinvent themselves halfway through, Soulcalibur III takes the crown. On the surface, it serves as the direct follow-up to Soulcalibur II's fast-paced, 3D weapon-based combat built around smooth 8-Way Run movement—familiar territory for anyone who loved the series on PlayStation 2.

Industry observers note that inside its signature Chronicles of the Sword campaign, however, the game fuses traditional one-on-one weapon duels with a real-time strategy game. You command squads across a tactical map, capture strongholds, and level up custom-built units—and by the second half of the campaign, early small-scale skirmishes escalate into complex, multi-front sieges against iconic series veterans and high-level bosses that test both your strategic planning and your blade skills.

Respect Your Elders: The London to Brighton Car Tour, Michigan Style

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the November/December 2026 concern of Car and Driver.
  • More than double that if you count Fresh Londons.
  • Industry observers note that maybe a few of you with an interest in early automobiles recognize the combination of London and Brighton from the long-running English vintage-car meet that travels between those two cities every November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the November/December 2026 concern of Car and Driver.

More than double that if you count Fresh Londons. There are about 30 Brightons, which I think means there are somewhere around 700 ways one could set up a London-to-Brighton antique-car run. Which, of course, is a totally normal thing to blueprint, right?

Industry observers note that maybe a few of you with an interest in early automobiles recognize the combination of London and Brighton from the long-running English vintage-car meet that travels between those two cities every November. First run in 1896 by an intrepid group of early—very early—car enthusiasts, the Emancipation Run was held to mark one of the first increases in speed limits: from single digits (4 mph) to a downright scorching 14 mph.

The London-to-Brighton event, or, as it’s now known, the RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run, looks like fun, so we decided to have a go between our own London and Brighton in Michigan with some antique American cars.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

Several things lined up well. Our course between London Township and the cute main street of Brighton was 57 miles, which is a good parallel to the U.K.’s 97-km (60-mile) route. Plenty of tree-lined country lanes connect the towns, a benefit when organizing a road trip for vehicles whose max speed may be more than 14 mph but still lags behind modern highway pace. Most crucial, there’s a fantastic community of early-20th-century-car collectors in Michigan, so finding folks who were willing to take out their Fords, Oldsmobiles, Pullmans, and REOs was no problem.

It has been revealed that what was a problem was finding a date. Every time I suggested a weekend, I’d get a flurry of texts and emails from the would-be participants. “So sorry,” said Mark Turner. “There’s a steam-car rally that weekend.” It might have also been Turner who couldn’t do another date because of a meet for vintage Bentleys. “I don’t know if I could do June 6th because we have an HCCA [Horseless Carriage Club of America] tour down in Georgia,” said Brent Terry, with apologies. Eventually, I just picked something and hoped a few of the crew would manage to fit it into their busy, brassy schedules.

An 1865 regulation required a flagger with a red warning cloth to walk ahead of any roadgoing mechanical vehicles and limited their max speed to just 4 mph on turnpikes and highways and 2 mph in cities, towns, and villages in the United Kingdom. The law was initially intended to apply to steam-powered road locomotives, which were growing in popularity in England and threatening traditional railways. As cars entered the chat, drivers chafed at the restrictions. An 1896 act of Parliament brought that speed limit up to 14 mph and was thus celebrated by English motoring clubs with a 60-mile rally, an annual tradition now under the 60-mile-long name of RM Sotheby’s London to Brighton Veteran Car Run.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

Industry observers note that michigan being Michigan, the day before our run brought pouring rain. It turns out vintage-car people are shockingly willing to brave weather. “I believe it rains a lot in England,” noted Rick Lindner. So, we showed up, as did eight shining examples of the earliest entries in American motoring, from a 1904 Ford Model AC owned by Lindner to a late-model 1913 Buick Model 31 helmed by Larry and Joyce Schramm. On the Car and Driver side, we brought doughnuts, passengers, and a lot of questions about old cars.

Industry observers note that after the third time I asked someone for the cubic-inch displacement of their engine, John Grace (who organizes his own vintage-car run in the fall and lent his 1911 Regal to teenage brothers Jonathan and Matthew Sinclair for our tour, and whose wife, Dorothy, once drove a Model T across America, making either one of the Graces very qualified to tell me what’s what in prewar car stuff) shook his head. He told me that while he can go look it up for me, owners of cars from this era don’t generally describe their engines in displacement. “We measure in horsepower,” he stated. “I never hear anybody ask about cubic inches for early cars.”.

It makes sense. In the modern era, cubic inches tend to reflect power output, but back in the days when a Curved Dash Oldsmobile might have a single jug measuring 95 cubic inches and making only four horsepower, it was more useful to announce your car’s 30 horsepower than, say, its 200 cubic inches.

Grace answered this, and all my other questions, with thoughtful enthusiasm, which is something I noticed about all the antique-car people I met that day.

“The older the cars, the nicer the people,” said Larry Schramm. For the hobby to have a future, he said, it needs younger people to ask questions and learn how to drive these cars. Plus, “we’re all in the same boat.” If your car isn’t the one broken on this run, it might be on the next.

In a recent development, antique-car drives are a bit like off-roading; it’s best to go in pairs so someone can pick you up and get you to the finish. That happened to Ted O’Dell, when his 1913 Buick Model 31 started running a temperature. When I talked to him about it, he was unbothered. Breakdowns are just a part of the process, as they were when the cars were newly introduced. It’s historically accurate to get a flat tire.

It has been revealed that even though I’d invited people through different contacts, most of the participants knew one another. Many of these owners have multiple cars, maybe a major four-door for longer tours and a Model T for local runabouts. They loan one another parts and cars and smudgy business cards for the one place that still sells horsehair upholstery stuffing.

Industry observers note that we all gathered in a parking lot across the street from Darana Dragway. The vehicle owners hunched over crank starters to coax engines into action amid a chorus of grunts and pops, both mechanical and human. Clouds of tire smoke drifted over from the drag-strip side as smooth-bodied race machines revved substantial V-8s to numbers that would reduce our two- and four-cylinders to steaming puddles of Babbitt. As an example of divergent evolution, it was stark, but a show of mutual interest implied that while the bodies and power outputs were different, there was a shared soul among us.

Once our great eight were puffing and clattering, we left the dragsters behind in our own clouds of smoke (oil, not tire). I rode in David Liepelt’s 1915 Model T Ford at the head of the line. For Liepelt and his T, this marks a return to C/D. They were the stars of our Model T versus Model S story back in February 2014, and Liepelt is still mad that then–tech director Don Sherman beat his Ford in a Tesla, so we let him lead the tour.

Recent findings suggest that liepelt set off at a pace that would have shaken the drivers of 1896. He was all limbs, pulling the throttle lever back to full acceleration, upping the spark advance, rocking the gear-selecting pedal into high, and adjusting his Ruckstell two-speed axle. It was like watching an octopus drive a car. I had to tell him to slow down to make sure we didn’t leave anyone behind. It’s impressive what 22 horsepower is capable of, and while acceleration wasn’t going to be the challenge, nobody in the early 1900s was much for a panic stop. “Not good, but better than nothing,” Liepelt noted as he barreled through an Ann Arbor intersection. If we were braking, I wasn’t aware. A line in my notebook reads, “It’s a very specific thrill to be in a car you could fall out of.”.

Thinking of joining the antiques road show? Here’s what to buy.

Industry observers note that affordability was a theme among the group, which may come as a surprise to people who’ve grown up hearing terms like “Brass Era” and “prewar” only in relation to megabuck Bugattis and Duesenbergs on concours lawns. Those cars still command massive prices, but more common brands have come down as older owners die and pass on to their family a garage full of acetylene headlamps and wood-spoke wheels. Our group was unanimous in suggesting a Model T as a gateway drug, including lensman James Lipman, who is now on his second T purchase (the first is shown above).

In a recent development, “The Brass Era ones may be worth $15,000 to $20,000,” said T owner Brent Allen. “But you can pick up a running T for sometimes $7000, $8000 easily.” Learning to drive a Model T is a challenge, but Allen said that shouldn’t put anyone off. Other owners will be eager to teach you, and there are so many reproduction parts. If you have a frame and an engine block, you can build a whole car from catalogs.

That thrill was a recurring theme. It’s the caress of wind in your hair like the first time you rode a bicycle. It’s the nervy pleasure of sitting the canter on a horse. It’s the very real possibility that you’ll never be able to stop. In a world where most cars can hit 100 mph before the end of an on-ramp, it’s amazing how exciting 35 mph can be when it takes all your extremities and maybe one or two of your passenger’s to keep the vehicle out of the nearest hedge.

Sources indicate that for Jonathan Sinclair, the youngest of our drivers at 16, learning on a vintage car ruined him for modern transportation. When he was told that he couldn’t take the driver’s test in the family Model T, his mom had to force him to do his remaining training hours in a newer car. “I don’t feel anything!” he complained. “After the involved process of driving an older car, you get in a modern car, and suddenly you don’t have to worry about anything. It feels odd.” He and his brother, Matthew, had been planning to bring their own project, a 1911 Brush, but then the Graces offered them the key to the Regal.

Our summer intern, Alayna Wilkening, joined the Sinclair brothers in the Regal, where she was given the job of watching the MotoMeter hood ornament for signs of overheating. Her official report was they experienced no difficulties aside from having to explain to multiple onlookers that the Regal was a Regal but not a Buick.

Recent findings suggest that behind them, senior news editor Caleb Miller was riding in luxurious and secure comfort, cushioned in the azure-blue cabin of Daniel Coffman’s 1910 Pullman. I noticed with no small amount of jealousy that he had a nice sturdy roof support bar to hold on to in the turns. His post-run report was that his desire to purchase a vehicle of this vintage has only increased with each exposure. He also rode back with Liepelt and declared the trip “probably the most exhilarating 53 mph I’ve ever experienced.”.

Editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga was spared the terror of Liepelt’s sporty T, instead getting the full touring-car experience in Wes Raynard’s flashy red 1909 Oldsmobile Model X3, which cost about $2000 when it was fresh. “This is the only one known to still exist,” Raynard told me. A quick look at past auction prices shows that the cherry Olds changed hands earlier this year for $55,105, which is considerably more than its original purchase price but a downright bargain to own a one-of-one survivor.

Recent findings suggest that “The ride is so smooth,” Quiroga told me at our rest stop. He looked mildly disappointed that things were going so well. “I was expecting the adventure to be more adventurous. All of these enthusiasts know their cars so well that they could tear down the entire thing and rebuild it on the side of the road. Only everything is working, and we’re ahead of schedule.”.

Despite Quiroga’s desire for more chaos, the overall consensus was that the inaugural C/D London-to-Brighton (Michigan) was a great success, and the gang plans to do it again in 2027. Barring any conflicts with the steam-car rally.

In a recent development, like a sleeper agent activated late in the game, Elana Scherr didn’t know her calling at a young age. Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them. Since receiving activation codes, Elana has written for numerous car magazines and websites, covering classics, car culture, technology, motorsports, and latest-car reviews. In 2020, she received a Best Feature award from the Motor Press Guild for the C/D story "A Drive through Classic Americana in a Polestar 2."  In 2023, her Car and Driver feature story "In Washington, D.C.'s Secret Carpool Cabal, It's a Daily Slug Fest" was awarded 1st place in the 16th Annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards by the Los Angeles Press Club.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep?
  • Industry observers note that the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake.
  • Researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, why does being awake for too long make us increasingly desperate for sleep? Scientists at the University of Basel in Switzerland have identified two groups of brain cells in mice that become more active the longer the animals remain awake. These neurons play a critical role in creating the pressure to sleep, offering new clues about how the brain regulates our need for rest.

Industry observers note that the longer we go without sleep, the more difficult it becomes to stay awake. This buildup of sleep pressure, often called sleep drive, helps ensure that extended periods of wakefulness are followed by longer and deeper sleep. Although sleep is essential for survival, exactly how the brain measures time spent awake and converts that information into an increasing need for sleep has remained a mystery.

Researchers led by Professor Alex Schier at the Biozentrum, University of Basel, have now identified brain cells that help regulate this process. The work was conducted in collaboration with scientists from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Auburn University.

"We have identified neuronal populations that monitor prolonged wakefulness and actively promote sleep," indicates Alex Schier. "This is an important missing piece of the puzzle in understanding why we become sleepy.".

Scientists Identify Brain Cells That Drive Sleep Pressure.

To investigate how sleep pressure develops, the team studied patterns of brain activity in mice under three different conditions: normal cycles of sleeping and waking, extended sleep deprivation, and recovery sleep. By comparing these patterns, they identified brain regions whose activity changed according to how long the animals had been awake.

In a recent development, within one of these regions, the brainstem, researchers pinpointed two groups of neurons involved in controlling sleep drive. Known as GABAergic and serotonergic neurons, both groups became progressively more active as the mice remained awake. Their activity then decreased once the animals fell asleep.

The next question was whether these neurons simply tracked how long the mice had been awake or actually helped create the growing need for sleep.

Experiments revealed that the neurons were directly involved in driving sleep. When researchers artificially activated both groups, the mice slept longer and more deeply, showing the same type of recovery sleep normally seen after extended wakefulness. When the neurons were inhibited, however, the animals slept substantially less and were able to remain awake and alert.

"These neurons do not simply signal that an animal has been awake," notes Schier. "Our experiments show that they are crucial to promote sleep, and that they may be key components of the neural circuitry that generates sleep drive.".

Sources indicate that the results provide particularly strong evidence that certain neurons activated during wakefulness do more than register lost sleep. They actively help generate the pressure that eventually pushes the brain toward sleep.

Mice Sleep 70% Less When Key Neurons Are Inhibited.

Industry observers note that further experiments produced an especially surprising result. When scientists suppressed both groups of neurons for an extended period, the mice slept approximately 70% less than normal.

Industry observers note that even more unexpectedly, most of these animals did not display some of the serious behavioral problems typically associated with prolonged sleep deprivation. Despite getting dramatically less sleep, many avoided impairments that researchers would ordinarily expect.

These findings suggest that the identified neurons influence not only the amount of time animals spend sleeping, but also how strongly the pressure to sleep increases during wakefulness.

Rather than simply responding to exhaustion, the brain appears to use specific neural circuits to actively regulate the growing need for rest.

A New Direction for Sleep Research.

Sources indicate that understanding these circuits could open important fresh avenues for studying sleep and its effects on the body. Researchers now hope to determine how the identified neurons communicate with other brain regions and what molecular processes allow them to generate sleep pressure.

Industry observers note that "Future studies could reveal how these neurons interact with the rest of the brain, and how sleep drive is generated at the molecular level," says Dr. William Joo, first author of the study. "Our ability to stably transform sleep behavior also allows us to explore adaptations to long-term sleep loss - this may eventually reveal ways to confer resilience to sleep deprivation and other physiological challenges.".

The findings establish that GABAergic and serotonergic neurons in the brainstem become increasingly active during prolonged wakefulness and play an essential role in promoting sleep.

It has been revealed that determining exactly how the brain makes sleep increasingly difficult to resist remains a major objective of sleep research. Beyond improving scientists' understanding of sleep disorders, this discovery could help explain how the nervous system adapts to extended wakefulness and other physical challenges.

Ultimately, a clearer understanding of the brain circuits responsible for sleep pressure could inspire new treatments and potentially reveal ways to improve resilience to sleep deprivation.

Materials provided by University of Basel. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that even though Toyota’s Hilux pickup truck is not sold on this side of the Pacific, most people have a pretty good idea about what it represents. Thanks to the antics in Top Gear in which they were drowned, blown up, and even set on fire, the Hilux has a reputation for being rugged to the point of near indestructibility. What you don’t expect is for them to be fast.

According to recent reports, of course, things are completely different in Southeast Asia, especially in Thailand. There, a pickup truck isn’t just a rough-and-tumble tool for work, it’s also a canvas for personal expression. Thai customizers turn their trucks into insane builds that would rival anything you’d find at Daikoku Parking Area in Japan or on the floor in Vegas at SEMA.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

Industry observers note that to put an exclamation point on the launch of its new Hilux Travo Z Edition, Toyota turned to its Australian design department. Said department reacted, to use the proper antipodean expression, by going off like a frog in a sock, building a Hilux that’s so crazy it’s not even really a pickup truck any more.

Industry observers note that the Hyper Z prototype features massively wide bodywork that struggles to contain 325/35 series tires on 22-inch wheels, and more aerodynamic elements than a small regional airport. There’s a table-sized front splitter, a diffuser out back, ground effects tucked under the body, and a park bench of a wing out back.

Industry observers note that also out back, an X-shaped wing that occupies the entirety of the pickup truck’s bed. Planning a run to your local DIY center? Whatever you’re picking up better fit in the glovebox.

Industry observers note that the standard Hilux Travo is powered by a 2.4-liter turbo-diesel engine good for 150 horsepower, but despite what looks like a huge Hilux-branded intercooler here, Toyota didn’t put any power numbers on the prototype. It’s more a love letter to Thailand’s custom truck culture, showing what can be done rather than what should be done.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps of more interest in a practical sense is how Toyota positions its Hilux in this market. Overseas, the truck is offered in both a high-floor and low-floor model, the latter riding low so that it is easier to load and unload for practical working conditions.

Conversely, in the U.S. market, pickups of all sizes have never been taller, which you’ll notice as soon as you need to load them up. Could Toyota successfully market a low-floor Tacoma model, one that’s a little easier to live with for commercial applications?

Industry observers note that either way, the Hyper Z Prototype is a cool way to shine a light on a slice of automotive culture that’s specific to a region. If you thought authentic Thai green curry was hot, just check out how spicy the country likes its pickup trucks.

EA Sports has revealed 3 upcoming Heroes coming to FC 26 Ultimate Team as part of Team 1 of the Winter Wildcards promo: Ivan Zamorano, Claudio Pizarro and Jill Scott.

In a recent development, the Bayern and Werder Bremen legend Claudio Pizarro is famously the Bundesliga’s oldest ever player, after turning out well past 40 years of age - up front no less. But he’s making an appearance in FC 26 because he won the Hero Vote Poll a few months ago, with the Peruvian edging out notable nutter Steffan Effenberg and the prolific Brazilian striker, Elber.

The love for South American Heroes continues with Ivan Zamorano presented in his Real Madrid guise rather than part of the unbelievably stacked Inter squad which featured legends and Icons ranging from current Atletico Madrid manager Diego Simeone to Javier Zanetti and Ronaldo Nazario.

And probably most interestingly, Queen of the Jungle and centurion Lioness, Jill Scott, is also coming to shore up the midfield with a card which fits the “Gullit Gang” pre-requisite of all face stats over 80 - including a dominant 91 physical befitting her role as one of the most recognisable enforcers in women’s football.

Whether her in-game body type will actually let her put that strength out on the pitch (she will surely also have Bruiser) remains to be seen, but she could easily have the gangly aura of Patrick Vieira if the rest of her PlayStyles are right.

New Ultimate Team Heroes have been added mid-season before, including the likes of Enzo Francescoli in FC 24, but 3 at once looks to indicate that EA is leaning on Heroes to add fan-favourite players to the game with a lower threshold than Icons.

Plus they can be given away for free without upsetting the power curve as much as Icons, as shown by the free Classic XI Heroes handed out recently (I got Mario Gomez, F).

The rest of the Winter Wildcards team features a host of equally famous, and now infamous, players with some featuring 99 stats and alternative positions.

Highlights include striker and CAM versions of Balon D’or holder Ousmane Dembele, but also everyone’s love-to-hate Low Driven Shot master, Claudia Pina.

There are also incredibly strong-looking Gabriel and Fede Valverde cards, as well as downgraded, and therefore hopefully cheaper, versions of Icons like Johan Cruyff.

#144940. 10 Side Modes That Became Bigger Than the Game They Came From

10 Side Modes That Became Bigger Than the Game They Came From

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I have always been enamored with the different ways that games have been brought to life, and Mods in particular have always felt magical to me.
  • Recent findings suggest that the same goes for bonus modes and custom maps that were never meant to be more than a fun extra.
  • Industry observers note that right, before you are all coming for me with pitchforks: Gwent never actually became bigger than The Witcher 3, and I have no qualms about admitting that straight away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I have always been enamored with the different ways that games have been brought to life, and Mods in particular have always felt magical to me. Someone, somewhere, loves a game so much that they start tinkering with it in their free time. Every now and then, that little side project ends up taking on a life of its own. Some of the biggest games in the world, including two of the biggest esports I write about, started out exactly like that.

Recent findings suggest that the same goes for bonus modes and custom maps that were never meant to be more than a fun extra. A few devs probably thought it would be fun to include a little bit of an extra to fans, or had an idea with limited resources that they wanted to give a try. Some of them went on to get their own releases, others created entire genres, and a few of them quite frankly outshone the game they were tucked away in. And in the spirit of that, let's take a look at ten side modes that became bigger than the game they came from.

Industry observers note that right, before you are all coming for me with pitchforks: Gwent never actually became bigger than The Witcher 3, and I have no qualms about admitting that straight away. Very few things could. The hype around it was something else, though: people happily ignored the end of the world to sit in taverns and play cards with every merchant, blacksmith and innkeeper they came across, and CD Projekt Red clearly noticed.

Industry observers note that the standalone version, GWENT: The Witcher Card Game, is something fans eagerly awaited. It did, however, come with its own sets of concerns. The version of Gwent it delivered displayed a few stark differences to the version people knew and fell in love with: It was free-to-play, quite competitive, and ultimately, a lot of fans simply never warmed to it. If you're after that original feeling, most people will point you towards Thronebreaker: The Witcher Tales instead.

According to recent reports, still, a card game from inside an RPG becoming popular enough to get its own release almost never happens. CD Projekt Red supported it until the end of 2023, and even then, it handed the game over to the community rather than switching it off. It didn't quite live up to the hype, but it absolutely earned its place on this list.

The Stanley Parable really shouldn't work as well as it does. You're an office worker, a narrator tells you exactly what you're doing, and it's up to you whether you want to listen to him. It's one of the funniest games I know, and it started out as a free Half-Life 2 mod that Davey Wreden released in 2011.

Wreden wanted to play around with what storytelling in games could be, and it clearly struck a nerve: the mod was downloaded more than 90,000 times in just two weeks. William Pugh then reached out about turning it into something bigger, and the two of them spent the next two years working on it entirely online. They only met in person a month after it came out, which is a detail to the origin story that I personally find quite charming.

Industry observers note that that remake released in 2013 and sold over 100,000 copies within a matter of days. Ultra Deluxe followed in 2022 and did the same within 24 hours.

It has been revealed that team Fortress 2 is so closely tied to Valve that it's easy to forget it didn't start there at all. It began as a Quake mod in 1996, made by three Australians, Robin Walker, John Cook and Ian Caughley, who had been inspired by a little Doom map they came across at LAN parties. Two teams, a bunch of very different classes, and everyone has a job to do. Sound familiar?

Valve liked it so much that it bought the rights and offered its creators jobs. Caughley remarked no, but Walker and Cook moved over, and Team Fortress Classic came out in 1999 as a mod for Half-Life. It then took until 2007 for Team Fortress 2 to finally arrive, with a cartoony art style that has aged better than most games from that year.

Industry observers note that once it went free-to-play in 2011, it became bigger and better. Somewhere between capturing the intelligence and pushing the payload, a huge part of the community became very, very invested in hats. I'm not judging, but I am a little bit scared of how much money has gone into them.

As someone who writes about esports, the lore behind Dota is one of my favorite tidbits of the gaming world. It all started with Aeon of Strife, a custom StarCraft map, which inspired a modder called Eul to make Defense of the Ancients for Warcraft III all the way back in 2003. Eventually, Eul made it open-source, and from there, it passed from hand to hand.

It has been revealed that the most popular version became DotA Allstars, made by Steve "Guinsoo" Feak, and when he moved on, the mysterious IceFrog took over. Guinsoo went on to help create League of Legends, which means one Warcraft III map is responsible for two of the biggest esports on the planet. What a wild family tree!

In a recent development, valve hired IceFrog in 2009, Dota 2 came out in July 2013, and the rest is happily ever after: it has been one of the most played games on Steam ever since. Truth be told, I love that the person who has shaped Dota more than anyone is still somewhat of a mystery. Somehow, that makes the whole thing even more feel like classic Dota.

Counter-Strike is one of the most influential FPS games ever created, but it doubled as probably the most impressive job application to exist. Minh "Gooseman" Le was in his last semester at university and wanted something that would help him get into game development, so he started working on a mod for Half-Life. Jess "Cliffe" Cliffe ran the website and the community, and the first beta came out in June 1999.

It has been revealed that every latest beta brought in more players, and by 2000, Valve had bought the rights and hired them both. From there, it was Source, Global Offensive and, in 2023, Counter-Strike 2, with the series becoming one of the biggest esports in the world along the way. Its Majors are still some of the biggest events in esports.

In a recent development, counter-Strike 2 still regularly sits at the very top of Steam's charts, with over 30 million monthly players. Gooseman, for the record, definitely got the job. I'd say it worked out.

According to recent reports, there was a point where it felt like every other game had zombies in it, and DayZ was right at the heart of that. It started out in 2012 as a mod for Arma 2, made by Dean "Rocket" Hall, and threw you into a huge open world full of the undead. The zombies were never really the scary part, though: other players were, because you never knew whether the person waving at you wanted to team up or take your tinned food.

Recent findings suggest that you needed Arma 2 to play the mod, so its popularity sent a three-year-old military sim right back to the top of Steam's charts. It reached a million players within four months, Hall joined Bohemia Interactive, and work began on a standalone version. Bohemia, quite understandably, was delighted.

That version released into Early Access in December 2013 and sold over two million copies in under six months, before its full release in 2018. I'll say this much: it hasn't moved all that far away from the mod, and that is a good thing. If you like survival games and don't mind a bit of betrayal, it's well worth your time.

According to recent reports, I’ll be honest, most of the Skyrim mods I personally perused have always been about silly things like turning every dragon into Thomas the Tank Engine. Those of you with more dignified taste, however, might be aware of The Forgotten City. It’s a time-travelling murder mystery set in an ancient underground city. Nick Pearce spent more than 1,700 hours on it, and it clearly was time well spent: the mod had over three million downloads, and an Australian Writers' Guild Award, the first time a video game had ever won one.

Pearce quit his job as a lawyer and rebuilt it as a standalone game with two other developers. It moved from Skyrim to ancient Rome, but kept its central idea: there is one rule, and if anyone breaks it, everybody pays. Steal from someone or hurt them, and the entire city is turned into gold.

Luckily, you get sent back to the start of the day whenever that happens, with everything you've collected so far. It's almost roguelike in that way, and every loop teaches you a little more about the people around you. I think it's one of the best detective games out there, and it started its life as a Skyrim mod.

Call of Duty: World at War was a very serious entry about the Pacific front of World War II, which is exactly why it's so funny that most people remember it for zombies. Treyarch hid Nacht der Untoten at the end of the campaign as an Easter egg, with no marketing behind it at all. You finished the story, and suddenly you were boarding up windows in a bunker whilst zombies tried to get in.

It was a hit straight away, so every map pack after that came with a new Zombies map. The first map didn't even have a story, but fans started building one anyway, and Treyarch eventually leaned all the way into it. The result is one of the most convoluted storylines in gaming, spread across multiple Black Ops games.

Zombies has been part of nearly every Call of Duty since, and these days, it's not unusual for it to be the main reason people pick up a Treyarch game at all. Quite the career for an Easter egg. Not even the developers saw that one coming.

Dota Auto Chess is the youngest entry on this list, and boy, did it blow up fast. Drodo Studio released it as a custom game inside Dota 2 in January 2019. You put Dota heroes on a chessboard, combine them to make them stronger and then sit back whilst they fight on their own, and the developers have actually mentioned that Mahjong was a significant inspiration.

Within months, it had over eight million players, and the substantial studios very quickly wanted a piece of it. Valve made Dota Underlords, Riot added Teamfight Tactics to League of Legends, and Blizzard brought Battlegrounds to Hearthstone. Drodo Studio, meanwhile, released its own standalone Auto Chess.

In a recent development, the hype has calmed down since then, but the auto battler genre is still very much here, and all of it traces back to one custom game. I find it quite funny that one of the biggest gaming trends of 2019 started out as just another option in Dota 2's custom games menu. Never underestimate a menu.

It has been revealed that the Binding of Isaac has a truly baffling amount of mods, and as someone that used to be utterly besotted with both the OG as well as The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, I have tried a large amount of them. A lot of them were high quality, but Antibirth was something else. Released by a group of fans in December 2016, it was basically an entire expansion: thousands of fresh rooms, nearly 100 new items and even its own soundtrack. It felt so much like Isaac that it was hard to believe it wasn't official.

Edmund McMillen clearly shared the fans’ feelings. He loved how well it understood the themes and style of his game, and rather than ignoring it, he started working with the team behind it. In 2018, he unveiled The Binding of Isaac: Repentance, the final DLC for the game, built on Antibirth.

In a recent development, repentance launched in 2021, with the Antibirth team helping to make their mod official, alongside a whole lot of upcoming content. I love that a fan project ended up becoming the final chapter of the game it was made for. Not many modders can say that.

America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • America's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up.
  • In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission.
  • America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America's electricity needs are growing rapidly, but the nation's aging power grid is struggling to keep up. More electric vehicles, increased electricity use in heavy industry, and the explosive growth of data centers are driving demand higher, putting additional pressure on an infrastructure system that is already falling behind.

In a Policy Forum paper published in Science, energy policy researchers from Carnegie Mellon University and the University of California San Diego warn that the United States faces one of the world's most serious bottlenecks in electricity transmission. The problem could have major consequences for electricity prices, grid reliability, and the nation's economic future.

America Is Building Just 10% of the Power Lines It Needs.

Industry observers note that A major concern is the extremely slow pace of transmission construction. Over the past five years, the continental United States has added an average of only about 500 miles of high-voltage transmission lines annually. Research suggests the country needs approximately 5,000 miles each year to triple the size of its interregional transmission network by 2050 and accommodate future electricity demand.

According to recent reports, that means the U.S. is building fresh high-voltage transmission lines at just one-tenth of the estimated pace needed.

High-voltage transmission lines serve as the highways of the electricity system, carrying large amounts of power over long distances from generating facilities to communities and businesses. Connecting regional grids allows electricity to flow more easily between areas, helping balance supply and demand when local power production falls short.

Studies have shown that larger, better-connected electricity networks can reduce costs for consumers while also lowering the risk of catastrophic blackouts. When one region experiences a power shortage, electricity from another region can help keep the lights on.

Despite these advantages, expanding the nation's transmission infrastructure has proved extraordinarily difficult.

The Biggest Obstacle Isn't Technology.

According to the researchers (Madeline Yozwiak, David G. Victor, and M. Granger Morgan), the main barriers to modernizing America's power grid are political and regulatory rather than technological.

Sources indicate that responsibility for approving major transmission projects is divided among federal agencies, state governments, local authorities, and private companies. Each has its own priorities and interests, creating numerous opportunities for proposed power lines to be delayed or blocked.

Existing electric utilities can also have financial reasons to resist stronger connections between regions. Greater competition from electricity suppliers elsewhere could weaken their influence over local markets, reducing the incentive to support projects that would benefit the broader electricity system.

As a result, even transmission projects that could lower costs and improve reliability across the country can struggle to gain approval.

Three Ways to Fix America's Power Grid Crisis.

To address the growing shortfall, the researchers recommend a three-part strategy combining stronger government action, modern transmission technologies, international cooperation, and regulatory reform.

1. Make better use of existing federal powers and advanced technologies.

It has been revealed that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Department of Energy (DOE) already have legal authorities that could help move important transmission projects forward. The researchers argue that these agencies should use those powers more effectively, including identifying transmission corridors of national importance and addressing disputes that prevent projects from receiving state-level approval.

Technological improvements could also dramatically increase the amount of electricity the grid can carry. One approach, known as reconductoring, involves replacing existing power line conductors with more advanced materials capable of transmitting more electricity without necessarily requiring entirely new routes.

Other advances, including newer High-Voltage Direct Current (VSC-HVDC) systems, offer additional ways to move large amounts of electricity efficiently. The researchers suggest that modern transmission technologies could double or even triple capacity.

Sources indicate that underground high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables offer another promising option. These systems can carry substantial amounts of electricity over long distances and could potentially be installed along existing highways and railroad corridors. Using these established routes could help avoid some of the land-use disputes and approval challenges that often delay conventional transmission projects.

2. Learn from countries that have already overcome similar obstacles.

The United States trails several international counterparts in building long-distance HVDC infrastructure and coordinating electricity transmission across regional and national boundaries.

Industry observers note that other countries have demonstrated that large transmission projects can move forward despite complicated political approval processes. Some have also successfully deployed underground HVDC systems on a large scale.

In a recent development, rather than developing every solution independently, the researchers suggest that the U.S. should study these international experiences and adapt approaches that have already proved successful.

One proposal is to establish an international forum involving electricity regulators and other experts, potentially led by organizations such as the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC). Such a forum could help American policymakers identify effective regulatory practices, planning strategies, and technologies used elsewhere.

3. Create a national commission to break the political deadlock.

The researchers also recommend establishing a Presidential-Congressional Transmission Commission to address the political and regulatory conflicts that have slowed grid expansion for decades.

Modeled on previous successful bipartisan commissions, the proposed group would bring together key stakeholders to negotiate difficult decisions and develop a coordinated strategy for reform.

Its responsibilities would include recommending changes to state and federal laws, examining whether FERC should receive broader authority over the locations of new transmission projects, and developing financial incentives for companies that lead new construction.

The commission could also recommend financial rewards for communities that host transmission infrastructure, helping ensure that local residents share in the benefits of projects that serve larger regions.

Why America's Power Grid Crisis Could Get Worse.

The researchers emphasize that the underlying challenge is not a lack of engineering solutions. Instead, the country's divided decision-making system allows individual stakeholders to obstruct projects that could deliver substantial nationwide benefits.

It has been revealed that "The fundamental challenge isn't technical, it's jurisdictional. Authority is divided among federal, state, and private entities, each with distinct priorities. When every stakeholder possesses the power to say no, even high-value projects that benefit the entire nation struggle to move forward," the authors warn.

Their assessment suggests that simply continuing with the existing system of overlapping regulations and fragmented authority will not be enough to meet America's growing electricity needs.

Without meaningful changes to how transmission projects are planned, approved, and built, the United States risks a prolonged infrastructure shortfall. The researchers warn that failing to resolve these problems could weaken electricity reliability and inflict lasting damage on the national economy, even as demand for power continues to climb.

Dually Noted: The Reasons Why Some Pickup Trucks and Vans Come with Dual Rear Wheels

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The term “dual rear wheels,” as applied to full-size pickup trucks and vans, raises as many questions as it answers.
  • In a recent development, you’ll often see so-equipped vehicles referred to in official specs or on a build sheet as DRW, as opposed to single-rear-wheel (SRW) pickups and vans.
  • DRW vans are usually the longest and tallest, used for both cargo and passenger hauling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The term “dual rear wheels,” as applied to full-size pickup trucks and vans, raises as many questions as it answers. Namely, one: Don’t all vehicles have two rear wheels? Good work, detective. The dual part, however, refers to the number of rear wheels on each side. Confusing? Sure. But consider yourself a member of an elite club. Send away for your decoder ring now.

In a recent development, you’ll often see so-equipped vehicles referred to in official specs or on a build sheet as DRW, as opposed to single-rear-wheel (SRW) pickups and vans. Out in the real world, you’re likely to observe dually pickups towing massive, heavy trailers, often using a gooseneck or fifth-wheel hitch.

DRW vans are usually the longest and tallest, used for both cargo and passenger hauling. Simply put, DRW vehicles are meant to handle big loads.

Industry observers note that automakers go the DRW route on configurations of their heavy-duty trucks and vans designed for hauling and/or towing heavy loads. Having those extra tires means more contact patch over which to distribute the weight. It’s the same basic principle that’s used on semi trucks—having 18 or so wheels spread across the semi tractor and its trailer allows the rig to carry literal tons.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

In a recent development, on dually trucks, the wider stance helps increase stability as well. You can think of the two extra wheels like outriggers, keeping the truck better planted in the face of crosswinds or in turns.

The main drawbacks of a dually setup are somewhat obvious. You have to worry about six tires instead of four, which in turn makes tire replacement more expensive. For dually trucks, the extra wheels sit outside the normal pickup-bed envelope, necessitating flared fenders to cover the extra rubber.

Sources indicate that maneuvering a big SRW truck or van is difficult enough. Predictably, the additional width of a DRW vehicle only adds to the challenge. It’s why many dually trucks end up with a blemish or two on at least one rear fender. The fenders of newer dually pickups are made from lighter-weight fiberglass instead of steel, so they’re less likely to bend and more prone to cracking when they meet a stationary object.

Industry observers note that this isn’t the case with most dually full-size vans. So-equipped vans add their additional tires inboard, which eliminates the need for flared rear fenders. The consequence of this arrangement is a slight reduction in outright cargo space due to the wheel wells extending further into the cabin.

Ever wonder why the front wheels of a dually truck or van have a severe outward dish to them? It’s so that all the wheels match and are therefore interchangeable should you need to use the spare. This dished design allows the rear wheels on one side to mate up with each other, which enables the use of two rear tires on both sides of the vehicle.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

The need for a dually comes down to capability. DRWs may be necessary to comfortably pull a fully laden horse trailer, a giant camper, various types of farm equipment, or the crops they help sow and reap. To get an idea of how much more a dually can handle, an SRW heavy-duty truck may be rated for a little more than 20,000 pounds of trailer weight on a bumper-mounted hitch, while the DRW variant of the same basic truck with a gooseneck hitch can pull almost twice the weight.

The difference isn’t as great with dual-rear-wheel versus SRW vans, mostly because both use bumper-mounted hitches. A DRW van may be able to tow as much as 50 percent more weight than a comparable SRW version. With some vans, towing capacity actually goes down when you add two rear wheels. Why go the dually route, then? Because that extra rubber is advantageous to rear-end stability—particularly when a van’s loaded up at, or near, its maximum payload capacity.

In a recent development, dually setups are available on heavy-duty versions of full-size pickups and some large vans. Those looking for a pickup truck with a bed can choose this setup on the Chevrolet Silverado HD, GMC Sierra HD, Ram HD, and Ford F-series Super Duty.

In the realm of enclosed passenger and cargo vans, only the Ford Transit and Mercedes-Benz Sprinter offer available DRW configurations. You’ll also often find DRWs in use on cutaway and chassis-cab versions of these trucks and vans, which are used in the aftermarket to build things such as box trucks, tow trucks, and RVs.

In some international markets, where full-size pickups are much less common, automakers produce DRW versions of their sub-full-size pickups.

Industry observers note that as with any towing or hauling exercise, make sure you understand the limits of your specific vehicle before loading it up or hitching a trailer to the back. Consider what you’re likely to tow or haul when shopping for your workhorse, and follow the manufacturer’s guidance on loading so you stay safe and avoid putting too much strain on the vehicle.

Dually is a term used for a pickup truck or van with dual rear wheels (DRW).

A dually pickup truck or van has two wheels and tires on each side of its rear axle for a grand total of four rear wheels and tires.

You do not need a CDL to drive a full-size pickup truck or an enclosed cargo or passenger van with dual rear wheels (DRWs).

Sources indicate that pedants will note that even a rear-wheel-drive dually relies on its engine to power four wheels (the four back ones). In a technical sense, however, a rear-drive dually is a two-wheel-drive vehicle, since power is sent to the drive wheels via two axle shafts. Similarly, though a four-wheel-drive-equipped dually may power a total of six wheels, the engine’s power only reaches the drive wheels via a total of four axle shafts (two at each end).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 2023, the Recording Academy has included an official category for video game soundtracks, adding an air of legitimacy to a diverse musical medium we know and love. Today, we learned the list of nominees for the 2027 Grammy ceremony, and it's an interesting lineup. The nominations are as follows:.

According to recent reports, as is often the case, what stands out most about these nominees is how, generally speaking, they don't fully align with gaming culture's favorite soundtracks of the year, and instead often trend toward the most recognizable IP (often franchises with films) of the year. On that note, it's most surprising to see that Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora has been nominated for the third year in a row: once for the base game, once for the Secrets of the Spires DLC, and now for the From The Ashes DLC. None of these soundtracks are bad by any means, but their Grammy representation far outweighs their cultural footprint.

Recent findings suggest that the standout here is Ghost of Yōtei, which is not an adaptation of the massive franchises the other games fall into. However, it's also a Sony-published game, which have a pretty good track record of getting nominations, potentially due to the organization's massive presence in the music and film industries. Still, Ghost of Yōtei has a great, unique score that's deserving of its spot, and also one previously nominated for best music at the 2025 Game Awards. The Grammys accept any releases between October 1 of one year and September 30 of the following year, so Ghost of Yōtei barely made the cut for this window. The Game Awards nominees will be revealed tomorrow – it will be interesting to see how much overlap there is between the categories.

Latest Update: A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open fresh possibilities for quantum technology.
  • Recent findings suggest that the material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented.
  • The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open fresh possibilities for quantum technology. Researchers have found compelling evidence of a rare magnetic state in which electrons behave in unexpected ways, even though the material produces no overall magnetization.

Recent findings suggest that the material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented. This behavior is associated with a phenomenon called p-wave magnetism, an emerging area of research that could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to controlling electronic properties.

The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound. Unlike many materials previously considered for studying this exotic form of magnetism, it offers researchers a practical way to investigate the underlying physics in detail.

An Unexpected Discovery in a Simple Metal.

It has been revealed that the research began about three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden, Germany. Dr. Erjian Cheng successfully grew high-quality single crystals of EuSi, providing the material needed for detailed experiments.

When researchers first examined the crystals using photoemission techniques, which probe the energies and behavior of electrons inside materials, they noticed something unexpected. The magnetic arrangement of the atoms had a remarkably strong influence on the electronic band structure, which describes the energy levels electrons can occupy and helps determine how a material conducts electricity.

According to recent reports, that observation raised an intriguing possibility. Could this simple compound contain an unconventional form of magnetism in which the spin of an electron is connected to the direction it travels?

According to recent reports, "When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons," explains Cheng. "That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.".

Industry observers note that answering that question required an international collaboration involving 38 scientists from 19 institutions. Participants included researchers from ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

A Strange Form of Magnetism That Cancels Itself Out.

It has been revealed that ordinary magnets, such as those attached to refrigerators, typically rely on a magnetic arrangement called ferromagnetism. In these materials, many electron spins align in the same direction, producing an overall magnetic field.

At temperatures between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, the magnetic moments of its europium atoms organize themselves into a repeating spiral pattern. These temperatures correspond to roughly minus 400 to minus 348 degrees Fahrenheit.

Each europium atom has a substantial magnetic moment, but their orientations balance one another across the spiral. As a result, the material has no net magnetization in this magnetic phase.

Recent findings suggest that however, the absence of overall magnetization does not mean magnetism has stopped influencing the electrons. In fact, the researchers found that the spiral arrangement produces a highly unusual electronic structure.

Industry observers note that in the proposed p-wave magnetic state, electrons traveling in opposite directions have opposite spin polarizations. Electron spin is a quantum property that gives electrons magnetic characteristics, although it should not be understood as an electron literally spinning like a tiny ball.

It has been revealed that the relationship between an electron's direction of motion and its spin is called an odd-parity spin texture. This means that reversing the electron's momentum also reverses the associated spin polarization.

Recent findings suggest that other materials can display spin-dependent energy differences because of a phenomenon known as spin-orbit coupling, which connects an electron's motion to its spin. In EuSi, however, the unusual spin structure appears to arise mainly from interactions between magnetic moments and the specific symmetry of their spiral arrangement.

Experiments Reveal Evidence of Rare P-Wave Magnetism.

To determine whether EuSi truly exhibits the predicted magnetic state, the scientists combined several sophisticated experimental methods with theoretical calculations.

Recent findings suggest that first, they used neutron diffraction, a technique that reveals how atoms and magnetic moments are arranged inside a material. These measurements confirmed that the europium magnetic moments form a spiral structure with the symmetry required for p-wave magnetism.

In a recent development, next, the researchers examined the material using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. This method measures the energies and momenta of electrons, allowing scientists to map the electronic structure.

The results showed that magnetic ordering substantially reorganizes the electron energy levels. In particular, the team observed magnetically driven energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts, indicating an unusually strong influence of magnetism on electron behavior.

The most decisive evidence came from spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which allowed the researchers to examine electron spin polarization directly.

They observed that the sign of the spin polarization changed across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. These zones are regions of momentum space used by physicists to describe how electrons behave within a repeating magnetic structure.

The team also found that spin polarization became much weaker near locations where theoretical calculations predicted the p-wave spin texture should disappear.

Taken together, the measurements provide compelling experimental evidence consistent with the predicted p-wave magnetic state in EuSi.

A Hidden Magnetic Spiral With Two Different Orientations.

The researchers uncovered another unusual feature of EuSi involving chirality, a scientific term describing handedness.

It has been revealed that A familiar example is the difference between a left hand and a right hand. They are mirror images, but they cannot be perfectly superimposed.

In a recent development, something similar happens with the magnetic spiral inside EuSi. Although the underlying crystal has a centrosymmetric structure, meaning its atomic arrangement is unchanged by inversion through a central point, the magnetic spiral can twist in either of two opposite directions.

These different spiral orientations create magnetic regions, or domains, with opposite handedness.

Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the scientists identified domains measuring approximately ten micrometers across. For perspective, ten micrometers is about one-tenth the thickness of a typical human hair.

When the researchers examined these regions using circularly polarized light, they detected different electronic responses depending on the handedness of the magnetic spiral.

This finding demonstrates that the direction in which the magnetic structure twists is linked to the material's electronic properties.

Sources indicate that "What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal," says Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. "This demonstrates how the discovery of new materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.".

Why This Discovery Matters for Quantum Technology.

One of the biggest challenges in studying p-wave magnetism has been finding materials that display the necessary magnetic properties while remaining practical for detailed experiments.

Earlier candidates have included insulating materials, as well as metals that develop the required magnetic order only at extremely low temperatures or have complicated symmetries that make their behavior difficult to interpret.

EuSi offers a particularly useful combination of characteristics.

Sources indicate that it is a stoichiometric metal, meaning its constituent elements occur in a fixed chemical ratio. Researchers can also grow high-quality single crystals of the material, and its spiral magnetic arrangement has the symmetry associated with p-wave magnetism.

Together, these features make EuSi a promising experimental platform for exploring how exotic magnetic states influence the behavior of electrons.

Sources indicate that theoretical studies suggest that metallic p-wave magnets could display several remarkable properties. For example, they may allow electrons with particular spin orientations to carry electrical currents without requiring an external magnetic field.

They could also produce strong changes in spin polarization when an electric current is applied, potentially offering latest ways to manipulate electronic behavior.

These possibilities are especially relevant to spintronics, a field of technology that seeks to use electron spin, rather than electrical charge alone, to process and store information.

Another intriguing possibility involves unconventional superconductivity, in which electrical current flows without resistance through superconducting states that differ from those found in conventional superconductors.

It has been revealed that importantly, these predicted effects have not yet been demonstrated in EuSi. The discovery does not establish that the material can already perform these functions, but it gives researchers a promising system in which to test the predictions.

More broadly, the findings highlight how much of a material's behavior can remain hidden beneath an apparently simple chemical composition.

A solid's properties depend on more than the elements it contains or how its atoms are positioned. The arrangement of magnetic moments, the symmetries they create, and the quantum behavior of electrons can also produce entirely unexpected effects.

By revealing compelling evidence of p-wave magnetism in EuSi, researchers have gained a latest opportunity to investigate these relationships and explore how unusual magnetic structures might eventually be used to control the electronic properties of future materials.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

Recent findings suggest that according to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Recent findings suggest that vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

In a recent development, zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Sources indicate that zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA mentioned in a statement.

“While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”.
