💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five.
  • Industry observers note that deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities.
  • There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, upcoming multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Industry observers note that deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Sources indicate that spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

Recent findings suggest that you can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

Sources indicate that as has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

Sources indicate that it's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

Acting as a follow-up to Deadlock's limited Halloween event, the newest update detailed on Deadlock's Steam Page brings countless balance changes, quality-of-life improvements, features, and some themed mechanics to get players into the holiday spirit.

According to recent reports, one of the most notable features of the limited-time event is a series of massive parade floats right outside the window, leading all the way down Blue Lane and visible right after loading into Deadlock's lobby. Aside from being simple decorations, these balloons also introduce a new mechanic by dropping Turkey dinners that can be collected for a new buff.

While the parade doesn't do much to start, after three minutes, refreshing crates will spawn hanging beneath them that drop the Turkeys when destroyed, alongside the chance of dropping additional goodies like buff items or Souls.

After eating a Turkey, you'll immediately gain two stamina and the 30-second Stuffed buff, granting you 5 percent Bullet Resist, 5 percent Spirit Resist, and progressively healing you for a total of 90 health. 20 minutes into a match, the health increase jumps to 90 instantly, and 170 over the 30 seconds.

You don't just want to go around eating every Turkey you can, however, as eating another while you have the Overstuffed buff will disable sprinting and give you 60 percent stronger gravity.

While the limited-time event is certainly a fun change, especially considering its real-life counterpart of the Macy's parade got delayed, the real meat (pun intended) of the update comes from the patch notes that have now gone into effect, with a few of the following changes being some of the significant highlights of the update:.

While these are only a small percentage of the changes introduced in the new revision, you can find all of the new adjustments on Steam's official Deadlock patch notes page, which also includes 166 individual nerfs, tweaks, and buffs, most of which affect the following heroes:.

While there are too many Deadlock changes to list them all here, I would definitely recommend checking out the patch notes if you play any of these characters or have had trouble facing them in the past.

According to recent reports, fnatic have signed Czech duelist Martin 'marteen' Pátek from Gentle Mates as their first new player for VCT EMEA 2027. The London club are rebuilding after missing Champions for the first time in the team's history.

The London club’s newly introduced duelist is a player who hurt them badly in 2026. Colin ‘CoJo’ Johnson is listed as manager of the rebuilt roster.

Industry observers note that the move still has one step left. Pley.gg listed the signing as still awaiting approval from Riot Games. The link is not latest. Word of a verbal agreement between marteen and Fnatic emerged on 24 September. That was about a month before Gentle Mates released their whole roster.

Fnatic have already seen what the duelist can do. Gentle Mates came out on top when the two sides met at the 2026 EMEA Kickoff. That win sent Gentle Mates to Masters Santiago.

It has been revealed that he led several stat categories in Santiago. Gentle Mates still went out 1–2 to AG and finished joint seventh to eighth. That result earned the team $35,000.

It has been revealed that the rest of Gentle Mates’ year was quieter. The team failed to qualify for Masters London or Champions Shanghai. Marteen still finished VCT EMEA Stage 2 as the team’s top-rated player, with a rating of 1.23. Signing a player who stood out in a non-qualifying side suggests Fnatic are building around individual firepower.

Fnatic’s own 2026 campaign ended earlier than planned. Joblife knocked them out with a 2–0 win in the VCT EMEA Stage 2 Play-Ins.

Sources indicate that the signing follows a clear-out of long-serving players. Boaster had been with Fnatic since 3 February 2021. Alfajer arrived on 9 May 2022, and crashies on 11 December 2024.

Recent findings suggest that marteen’s own spell at Gentle Mates ran from 20 November 2025 to 25 October 2026. The two rosters are now tied together by the same transfer window.

According to recent reports, gentle Mates had already cleared their own decks. All five players on the active roster and both coaches were let go before the club’s first season as a VCT partner team.

For a British organisation, the swap leaves Fnatic’s identity in fresh hands. Boaster had been the longest-serving name in the departing group. Kaajak and Cloud are now the continuity, with marteen as the headline addition.

Recent findings suggest that fnatic do not need to qualify for the opening event. The club is one of eight EMEA partner teams for 2027, and each partner goes straight into Kickoff. Places at later events must be earned. Four teams from Open Qualifiers complete the field.

The first chance to see both rebuilt sides comes soon. The 2027 EMEA Kickoff, featuring 12 teams, runs from 14 January to 7 February 2027 at the Riot Games Arena in Berlin. Its top three teams will qualify for Masters Seoul, the first international event of the 2027 season.

In a recent development, after weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

Industry observers note that we’re expecting a content patch each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one newly introduced map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

According to recent reports, while we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

According to recent reports, january’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a latest matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Sources indicate that things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Industry observers note that interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a latest Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another fresh Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

According to recent reports, finally, April is when the significant guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1491 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a latest physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

For Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

On release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

However, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

The answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "People were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

In the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for users. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

Recent findings suggest that "I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he states. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find new uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

In a recent development, when looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal owners: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the issue of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

All the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got big as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Sources indicate that alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering customers.

In a recent development, "I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The previously revealed demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.
  • Sources indicate that unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously revealed demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Sources indicate that unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically rolled out first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

Recent findings suggest that the Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Recent findings suggest that another major reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

And if you're not quite sure where to cast your votes, here's why this action-packed RPG might just be your best bet.

Industry observers note that intuitive touchscreen controls aside, there's also the motion sickness reduction mode along with the customisable UI, offering more freedom for players to tinker around with button sizes and transparency to suit their preferences. This comes on top of the massive open-world scale that's not just a "lite" version of the PC version but the full experience on mobile - and with cross-progression to boot.

A dedicated community, and an even more dedicated team Speaking of the player base, adventurers have been diving into this Wuxia-themed world since the mobile version released on December 12th last year, topping the charts on iOS' free downloads across 60 regions.

Over a whopping 100 million players have built a community around Where Winds Meet throughout the globe, and it's all thanks to the equally dedicated development team that's constantly releasing massive updates to keep the momentum going.

The first of many massive anniversaries to come And if you haven't been keeping up with the latest, Where Winds Meet is right now celebrating its first anniversary festivities with the Hutuo enhancement, pushing the RPG to skyrocket to the 4th spot on the top-sellers chart on Steam. It bagged 7th place on Twitch on November 13th, hitting its peak of 70,000 concurrent viewers.

Recent findings suggest that it's not just the Dual Spears Martial Art combat and the Hutuo storyline players were keen to sink their teeth into - the Horse Racing Chess and Jianghu Tactics also offered everyone more casual ways to get into the action with the latest update. Plus, more than $150's worth of goodies were given away, with more to expect before the year ends.

No better time than now Given that the PC and console versions were released globally on November 15th, 2025, that means that only the global mobile version is eligible for The Game Awards this year. It still boasts the same uncompromising quality across all platforms, regardless of the category.

Suffice it to say that Where Winds Meet is poised to win major at The Game Awards, and if you'd love to show your support, you can vote for the Eastern fantasy adventure and make your voices (and your choices!) heard at the awards ceremony ahead of December 10th!

Download now! Where Winds Meet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.
  • In a recent development, the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • It has been revealed that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a new motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

In a recent development, the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

It has been revealed that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a new motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

"But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

You know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which currently looks likely to last until at least 2028.

Breaking: The Most Loved and Hated JRPGs by Fans

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan.
  • However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided.
  • I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan. Fixed characters, linear narratives, creative progression, and an atduesthetic usually inspired by anime are what tell us at a glance what makes a JRPG stand apart from any other subgenre under the role-playing umbrella. And to be honest, those exact elements are what draw me to the genre, sometimes removing one or adding another.

However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided. Some titles seem to sit at the same level of love and hate for fans, no matter which side you're on. That is why I decided to talk today about the most loved and most hated JRPGs by the public. This isn't a consensus or an objective truth, but a fun look at what I have observed after years on forums, debating with fellow JRPG lovers, and tracking the fanbase's overall perception.

I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.

While I couldn't find a direct primary source confirming this claim, outlets like Kotaku and RPGFan say the same thing: due to Xenosaga Episode II flopping so hard, the series was cut from its intended six episodes to just three. For fans hoping to see Tetsuya Takahashi's vision fully realized, that was a massive blow and certainly left a mark of hatred on the second Xenosaga.

According to recent reports, while Xenosaga Episode I: Der Wille zur Macht went over budget and featured far more cinematics than the average JRPG player was accustomed to (yeap), it was still a satisfactory experience. The second one? Not so much. The shift in art direction and the battle system genuinely pushed players away and, allegedly, led Bandai Namco to safeguard its investment by wrapping up the entire story as a trilogy. Much like Xenogears, Xenosaga became a beautiful what-could-have-been scenario, though luckily we eventually got to see Takahashi's ambitions realized with Xenoblade, which is still going strong.

Recent findings suggest that to be completely honest, I am not that major of a fan of EarthBound. I played EarthBound Beginnings, also known as Mother, and found it impressive for an NES JRPG. Shortly after, I moved on to EarthBound, which I had played a long time ago and didn't remember much, and I walked away unimpressed. Maybe the American parody didn't resonate with me (I am not American), or maybe I played it too late, and the cultural zeitgeist didn't hit me the same way.

Even so, I fully recognize how much people who enjoy this JRPG truly adore it. They spare no praise, speak fondly of the experience, and admire not only the game itself, but also its creator, Shigesato Itoi. Many of those fans claim Mother 3, a title that never officially left Japan, is even better, but since I didn't vibe with the second entry, I have little interest in trying it.

Sometimes a game is hated for its themes, other times for an overly boring battle system, or perhaps because of an obnoxious character we cannot stand looking at. Occasionally, however, games draw hatred simply for feeling apathetic, failing to spark any real emotion in the player, and offering nothing particularly remarkable. That's exactly the case with Tales of Zestiria for many Tales fans.

Mind you, I actually enjoy the game, and it was the very first Tales of title where I earned the platinum trophy. I was never overly critical of Sorey's journey, the complex equipment fusion system, or even the misleading marketing around Alisha's protagonism. I mean, okay, fair enough, those all sound like completely valid points of criticism, yet I still had a good time. Not everyone can say the same, and whenever you look at a Tales of tier list, Zestiria almost always sits right at the bottom.

Apparently, there are two types of fans in the JRPG world: those who love Suikoden II and those who haven't played it yet. I am not kidding here. I considered adding Xenogears to this spot because I know it has a very vocal fanbase, quite scary to be honest, borderline toxic. But Suikoden? That feels like a genuine relationship, a true love situation. Every time you meet someone who notes Suikoden II is their favorite game, you can practically see their eyes light up.

According to recent reports, to a large extent, I get it! Suikoden II is awesome. The grounded political plot stood out at a time when countless games were mostly about slaying God in a high fantasy setting. The 108 recruitable characters, each carrying their own motivation and reason for joining the resistance. The six-party-member battles with combo skills, and so on. Okay, you might need to use a walkthrough to recruit everyone and unlock the true ending, but the journey itself is already wonderful, and Luca Blight is a terrific villain. What is there not to love, right? Glory to Suikoden.

According to recent reports, there is nothing more miserable than watching a series you love, follow closely, and appreciate in every detail slowly fall from grace. For me, that didn't happen with Star Ocean, because I genuinely love Star Ocean: The Divine Force, though that is precisely how many felt after Star Ocean: Till the End of Time, the third entry. Plenty of fans didn't care for Star Ocean: The Last Hope yet could still stomach it, but Star Ocean: Integrity and Faithlessness? Just mentioning the name makes me feel your glare.

According to recent reports, the fifth Star Ocean suffered from an affliction that hit many JRPG franchises during that era: constricting budgets. I know that doesn't excuse its final quality, but it is the reality. The game severely lacked traditional cutscenes, playing out almost entirely through real-time in-engine camera angles, not out of artistic charm, but due to a lack of investment. I still like the game for two reasons: Item Creation remains incredible, and as someone who loves constantly swapping between party members, being able to deploy everyone into battle at once was a blast, even if having seven party members acting simultaneously got confusing and felt like a bit too much. It had a chaotic family reunion vibe, you know.

It has been revealed that out of all the JRPG fans I know, well over half say they discovered or fell in love with the genre after playing Final Fantasy VII. That fact alone could summarize this entire entry, because you either know someone just like that or you are that person yourself. I am a bit older, so I played other JRPGs before FFVII, though my cousin fits that exact mold, since he still uses an email address with the game's acronym in his handle to this day.

It is completely understandable, mind you. Final Fantasy VII was a global phenomenon that paved the way for JRPGs to gain worldwide recognition. That is why if you watch footage from the E3 showcase where the remake was unveiled, you will see countless explosive reactions. I know many newcomers to the genre or franchise don't understand why Square Enix split the remake into three parts, calling the firm mercenary (fitting for the game's plot, to be honest). Yet, I believe Square did it to honor the franchise's legacy, deliver something fresh for longtime fans, and naturally attract a new audience who can experience that same magic veterans felt when they first played and fell in love with it.

Whereas with most entries I listed as most hated (not hated by me, remember!) I tried to soften the blow and use euphemisms to avoid insulting people who enjoy those games or the developers behind them. For Lunar: Dragon Song, though, the gloves are completely off. I had only heard rumors about it, about how this mechanic was terrible and that feature was lousy, until one day I decided to test it for myself.

Good lord, it is awful. So many baffling design decisions make me genuinely wonder how anyone let them pass. First, and most obviously, simply running in the game drains your HP. I mean, what? Then there are two separate reward modes per battle, one granting only experience points and another granting only loot. I didn't understand that system at first and left loot mode active, feeling bizarrely weak despite fighting endless battles. On top of that, combat has mandatory auto-targeting, plus a bland story, forgettable characters, and other uninspiring features. Lunar: Dragon Song is universally hated, and it deserves every bit of it.

Recent findings suggest that whenever someone asks me which JRPG I would recommend to a complete newcomer to the genre, the answer nine times out of ten is Chrono Trigger. Pointing to a 1995 release even today speaks volumes about the work's enduring relevance and timelessness. And I will go a step further: that recommendation doesn't rely on cheap nostalgia alone, because Chrono Trigger truly is a spectacle, with pacing, gameplay, and design that can captivate even the most stubborn skeptics who resist JRPGs.

Industry observers note that and of course, among JRPG enthusiasts, it is tough to find anyone who doesn't genuinely love Chrono Trigger. You might have critiques about it (I certainly do), or complain about one small detail or another. Still, it's nearly impossible to deny that it is a masterpiece and a majestic blueprint for building a JRPG. It stands undeniably as the most beloved JRPG of all time, even if you don't happen to be one of the people who love it.

The MOBA genre is competitive in every sense and Quantic Dream is trying to break into it with a Magic the Gathering-esque spin on the format. Players build a deck of cards before queuing into teams of 3, then face off as battling mages, summoning creatures, building fortifications and casting spells rather than choosing a Hero with unique abilities in the traditional MOBA style.

Beta content includes a newly introduced map, 6 new spells and 5 new summon creatures for your deck, as well as 3 new buildings too.

Also newly introduced for this second closed beta is an introduction and tutorial for some of the game’s finer details, as well as a text chat for strategising and much-needed player reporting system to go with it. Recent findings suggest that despite missing out on the Game of the Year slot, however, PlayStation still features in other categories. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.

Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an issue for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming patch, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another massive content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest revision brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a latest narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

In a recent development, the major fresh story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

Sources indicate that these are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

Industry observers note that the Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

Sources indicate that the other massive addition in 2.2 are the two fresh 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

In a recent development, chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

Recent findings suggest that as with every major enhancement, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

If you’re jumping back into the game soon, be sure to hit up our Infinity Nikki codes page for some freebies.

In a recent development, hornet might be the hero in Silksong, but the award for most beloved character in the Hollow Knight sequel almost certainly goes to Sherma. You meet the optimistic little bug early on in your journey and bump into them frequently throughout. You know they’re nearby because of the catchy tune they’re always singing.

Mario Wonder’s Talking Flower toy serves as evidence of that.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spoilers for the end of Mass Effect 3 follow, naturally.
  • Recent findings suggest that you know what?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers for the end of Mass Effect 3 follow, naturally.

Recent findings suggest that you know what? I didn't have many questions left at the end of Mass Effect 3. Joker was a robot now. His robot girlfriend was perhaps less of a robot? Shepard converted herself into a dotfile to make the Reapers chill out, and Buzz Aldrin's talents lie in areas other than voice acting.

It has been revealed that I had plenty of questions when BioWare unveiled Mass Effect 5 was gonna be a thing though. Could you really write a Mass Effect story in the radically changed galaxy we were left with at the end of Shepard's adventure? Apparently, you could. In a recent AMA on Reddit (via IGN), BioWare writer Cat Valente wrote that the now-cancelled Mass Effect sequel's team put a lot of work into handling ME3's endings "in a way that wouldn't piss everyone off, [or] at least not piss them off completely".

The goal, says Valente, was to write a continuation of Mass Effect's narrative that "wouldn't privilege any one kind of player over another". That tracks with what we've heard before: leaks have suggested ME5 was set to more or less wrap all the previous game's endings into one (Deus Ex: Invisible War style, hell yeah).

In a recent development, of course, it'd have to do that while allowing BioWare "to actually write a coherent story going forward, within the limits of having to do it in a playable mainstream videogame and not a post-modern 3000 page novel", adds Valente. "Not for nothing, guys, but that's *kind of a tall fucking order*. Part of the reason it took so long and Andromeda was in Andromeda is that figuring out an elegant solution to that problem turns out to be *really hard*".

The sheer challenge of creating a coherent, satisfying follow-up to ME3 that took into account everyone's choices had Valente, at one point, "thinking *god, if I'd known when I finished ME3 that I'd be one of the people who had to find the mops and buckets to clean up that mess...*".

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, she reckons the studio did eventually alight on a way of handling it that made sense. "Yes, there was an answer, yes, I know it, as least inasmuch as I know what it was when I was working there… We knew all the discourse on the endings, of course we did, and I do think as a fan I would have been happy with the solution (at least what it was when I left) if I booted up the game having had nothing to do with it".

And, well, that's that. We'll never know if the internet would have been satisfied or not (though I know where I'd put my money on that question), because EA killed the project and BioWare with it, and there's rarely a follow-up to an ending like that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hours before it's even playable in most of the world, Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken the record for the most viewers across livestreaming platforms like Twitch.

According to streaming data and analytics website Streams Charts, GTA 6 had amassed 6.38m live viewers across Twitch, YouTube, and Kick at 12:30 UTC today. At that time, the game had been officially available for a few hours in Upcoming Zealand, and elsewhere by using a region-switch trick.

The previous record for most live viewers was set by Valorant, Riot Game's popular tactical shooter, during its closed beta in xx. That game brought in 1.74m live viewers, but it's worth noting there was a promotion offering players a chance to access the beta if they watched a stream. Despite having no such incentive, GTA 6 has more than tripled Valorant's record.

According to recent reports, twitch is the largest platform for GTA 6 streams according to Streams Charts, and already the game is the 6th biggest category in Twitch history. It's also expected the figure will increase as GTA 6 launches officially in more regions of the world.

If you'd like to find out when exactly Grand Theft Auto 6 releases for you, check out Eurogamer's GTA 6 launch time guide for an accurate list by country. Breaking: Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game.
  • It has been revealed that the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

It has been revealed that the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

Sources indicate that it makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

It has been revealed that thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

Industry observers note that it's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

It has been revealed that in terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program has delivered a tonne of information about the game’s big upcoming update, Version 2.6. This latest addition kicks off celebrations in New Eridu, and it’s dubbed Encore for an Old Dream.

Recent findings suggest that version 2.6 is not far off, either, arriving in ZZZ on February 6 - exactly one week from today. Encore for an Old Dream is something of an in-between story that takes place after the end of Season 2.

Industry observers note that the narrative of 2.6 sees the Proxies’ return to Sixth Street for Newly introduced Eridu's annual Gilded Carrot Day. At the centre of the celebrations is the debut of idol group Angels of Delusion at the 404 Error music venue, but not all is as it seems.

Industry observers note that the story follows the Proxies getting invited backstage to support the group, which also includes helping them set up practice schedules, organise events and manage social media activities. There’s a rhythm minigame as part of that, along with upcoming maps and mechanics for Marcel Adventure.

Angels of Delusion is also the group that the two newly introduced Agents being introduced in this patch belong to. Members of the same group are capable of performing coordinated attacks. The new arrivals are Sunna and Aria.

According to recent reports, sunna is a an S-Rank Physical Support Agent who specialises in boosting teammates using Attack and Anomaly. Her Ultimate sees her pull out a giant hammer to land heavy damage, and bring teammates into combat using Quick Assist. Sunna’s companion, Bubblegum, can cast Cat's Gaze on enemies, marking them for detonation. Bubblegum can also buff the squad’s attack.

Aria is the other new arrival, the group’s lead vocalist who can shift between two forms, idol projection and construct. Aria is an Ether Anomaly Agent who also deals high burst damage, specifically against enemies who suffer from any Attribute Anomalies.

Sunna and Aria also benefit from the support of the amusingly named Bangboo Biggest Fan, a fan club president who can heal them over time, and boost the squad’s Attack any time two or more Angels of Delusion members are present.

Version 2.6’s S-Rank re-runs are Yixuan (Auric Ink - Rupture), and Yuzuha (Physical - Support), who you can look forward to as part of the banners.

Version 2.6 will also expand Hollow Zero with a new game mode, Operation Matrix. The mode offers themed stages that rotate weekly, each offering new mechanics. You can now also Sweep in Hollow Zero.

Recent findings suggest that beyond all the celebrations, this update also brings combat kit overhauls to a couple of older S-Rank characters, Lycaon and Harumasa. You can look forward to multiple limited-time events, too, including one where you can earn a new outfit for Pan Yinhu.

Sources indicate that the major event is naturally going to be themed around Gilded Carrot Day, and it actually starts today. There’s the usual run of login rewards (about 3,300 Polychromes), as well as daily activities. Yet another login event - Gilded Surprise, Wonderful Boo-ns - will be available February 14-23, offering daily draws from a pool of 4 billion Polychrome.

As always, there’s no reason not to catch up on the latest set of Zenless Zone Zero codes for some free in-game items.

Tech Report: Ubisoft Claims It Encourages, But Doesn’t Require Generative AI Usage During Game Development

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as AI usage during game development and discussions surrounding it become more prominent, Ubisoft has been taking a firm stance on embracing it.
  • According to a report yesterday from Vertical Slice, the organization has been enforcing generative AI usage across its development teams in order to increase productivity and enhance the project in general.
  • However, Ubisoft has now responded to the original reporting, stating that while they do encourage AI usage across all production stages, it doesn’t mean that they require every single project to implement it, as they still need to be added only when it actually makes sense.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as AI usage during game development and discussions surrounding it become more prominent, Ubisoft has been taking a firm stance on embracing it. But according to the firm itself, the usage of such tools is more like a suggestion than a rule to be strictly followed.

According to a report yesterday from Vertical Slice, the organization has been enforcing generative AI usage across its development teams in order to increase productivity and enhance the project in general. And if you choose not to implement it, you would have to justify your choice.

However, Ubisoft has now responded to the original reporting, stating that while they do encourage AI usage across all production stages, it doesn’t mean that they require every single project to implement it, as they still need to be added only when it actually makes sense.

Recent findings suggest that the original version of Vertical Slice’s report states that, after speaking with various employees (who chose to remain anonymous due to possible backlash), Ubisoft is looking forward to increasing its gen-AI usage across all titles. If they choose not to use it, they have to detail the reasons for their choice. Otherwise, their ideas wouldn’t be approved to be worked on.

The report came out days after Ubisoft confirmed that their newest studio, Motherbrain, would be an AI-focused studio, being an key part of their “fresh operating model”. The announcement also came days after over 160 staff members were let go from their positions in Canada-based studios.

According to Ubisoft, they are simply encouraging their “teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work.”.

While it all seems daunting and terrifying, the studio decided to step up to clarify exactly what it all means. According to Ubisoft, they are simply encouraging their “teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work,” and ensuring that no employee is being silently forced to implement gen-AI in their work.This aligns with a claim from one of the employees Vertical Slice spoke with. According to them, while they aren’t outright mandated to use AI in their projects, the tech giant has fully decided to implement it whenever they have the chance.

While "AI psychosis" has been a thing for a while, it’s undeniable that the existence of generative tools has greatly shifted the industry and its inner workings in just a couple of years. From waves of layoffs followed by AI-pilled initiatives and the implementation of disclaimers about its usage on official game store pages, it’s hard not to be alarmed by all of these signals.

Sources indicate that ubisoft has been a huge player in these changes. The new Motherbrain studio is a byproduct of Teammates, an AI experiment from last year. This AI-powered demo uses the tool to mold your experience according to your voice and actions, as NPCs will react to your commands and, as stated on their official site, “allow players to experience the story in their own way”.

With all of these new advances in mind, it’s not unexpected to see such a posture from the manufacturer. However, it doesn’t mean they should be free of criticism when it's due. It’s hard not to associate all of the previously mentioned layoffs (which have been ever more common in the industry) with the increasing fear of being replaced by AI.

Another Ubisoft employee also mentioned feeling “cornered by generative AI all the time” since the recent attitude shift from the higher-ups, implying that some pressure over AI usage does exist inside the organization.

This doesn’t mean that Ubisoft’s own statement is incorrect. It could simply be a different way of perceiving attitudes and decisions taken by the company. But with so many AI-related incidents across the industry, such as the recent wave of AI game copies, it’s hard not to be worried about the future of gaming.

Pocket monsters, just not those ones.

Industry observers note that pre-registration only opened at the end of October, so Bandai hasn't kept anyone waiting long. Digimon Alysion is out now on iOS and Android, finally putting the Digimon Card Game on your phone.

Expect an original story with a brand new cast of characters, plus a few Digimon you won't have come across before. It's built to teach you the rules as you play through it. The tutorial covers how cards are laid out and used, along with the basics of a battle.

Industry observers note that your collection mixes cards from the physical Digimon Card Game with latest ones made for Alysion. On top of that, you’ve got Shiny Cards, Alt-Art Cards and Premium Alt-Art Cards (the animated ones), and you'll get one free pack a day to build your decks from.

Once you’ve fleshed out your kit, you can take it into ranked against people from around the world, or keep things relaxed and spar against friends and characters from the story instead. Breeding is back as well, for that matter. You can raise Digimon and Digivolve them all the way up to Mega, and there's a Digidex of more than 100 entries to fill in.

According to recent reports, pokémon TCG Pocket is the obvious comparison, and probably the reason Digimon Alysion is arriving now at all. The difference is that Bandai isn't starting from scratch, and if you've been playing the physical version, you'll recognise a fair bit of what’s part of your packs.

Bandai has already done something similar with Dragon Ball's Fusion World, which you can play digitally and on paper, so it's a fairly safe bet the game is meant to send some people towards the physical cards too.

Digimon Alysion is free-to-play with in-app purchases on the App Store and Google Play, and a launch event, Battle Carnival Dukemon Ver., is running now.

Industry observers note that unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that strategy release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the firm has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental issues.

Unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

Industry observers note that the grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 isn't even out yet, and it's already causing some technical problems over at the game's official Reddit page.

In a post verified by r/GTA6 moderators and pinned to the page, user and moderator PapaXah wrote "GTA 6 broke Reddit", and explained that "many things" were right now busted at the time of the post. Looking through Reddit, many flairs (little labels attached to posts) aren't loading properly and appear as a string of code rather than proper images. PapaXah also replied to one user suggesting they make real flairs based on these busted flairs, writing: "Reddit's so broken I couldn't even do it. We actually have a bunch of newly introduced flairs that I can't even upload.".

Another moderator, TekS, also acknowledged that some user's posts may not be viewable as a result of ongoing strain on Reddit during GTA 6's release. They commented: "If you can't post/comment or see your user flair, well, know that it's perfectly normal.".

Starsand Island is a life and farming sim that isn't gacha, and it's out next week

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that though it may seem like we just had a massive life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

According to recent reports, the game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

Seed Sparkle Lab declared today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

The developer said to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access.

Starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

In a recent development, speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese Newly introduced Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

Industry observers note that on top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab says you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

In a recent development, you can look forward to more Starsand Island coverage from us in the near future. Until then, you can get started by planning who you’re going to date now.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"To help alleviate server congestion following the release of Patch 8.0, we will be enabling cross-region Data Center Travel between the North American and European data centers during scheduled maintenance on Tuesday, December 1, 2026.

"… We will continue to take community feedback into account as we carefully evaluate the possibility of permanently enabling travel between the North American and European data centers, as well as opening travel between other physical data centers," via the Lodestone.

This is a massive deal and I'm very excited.

I play Final Fantasy 14 on the US servers—which is a problem, because I live in the UK. I do so because, well, some of my closest friends are on those servers, too; but also because there's a slightly livelier roleplay community bustling on the US side of things, and I'm a roleplayer who likes squeezing my warrior of light like he's a stress toy.

In a recent development, as a result, I've often stared longingly at the people who play in the UK due to the crime of my time zone: Unable to play with my UK friends, unable to join a static raiding group that starts at a reasonable hour, and unable to play the game without terrible animation lock on my abilities. Unless I, say, broke ToS and used an addon that brought me on-par with people who have 30 ping, hypothetically. Which I don't do.

Square Enix has thrown open these doors, however, to mainly deal with congestion troubles:.

It has been revealed that "As peak play times differ between North America and Europe, another physical data center may be less crowded and serve as a viable option when login queues on your usual data center are long. While players connecting from geographically distant locations may experience increased latency, we encourage you to try playing on a different physical data center before the expansion rolls out.".

However, they know that people like me have expressed their yearning to hop between the good ol' USA and Europe: "However, we have received ongoing feedback from players wishing to travel between the North American and European data centers, and many players in both regions are able to communicate in English even when it is not their first language.".

Sources indicate that all in all, this'll be a huge quality of life improvement. There might be some difficulties, though: raiding culture can vary drastically even between logical datacenters like Aether and Crystal, let alone between continents. However, I'd be shocked if the differences between US and EU raiding cultures were insurmountable; JP and US? Might be a bigger deal.
